reference.source: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
clinicalPearls: A burst fracture of the ring of the atlas (C1), classically a four-part fracture of the anterior and posterior arches produced by axial loading
Axial compression (a dive or a blow to the vertex) drives the occipital condyles onto the sloped lateral masses, splaying them apart and breaking the ring
Stability depends chiefly on the integrity of the transverse atlantal ligament
The rule of Spence uses combined lateral mass overhang on the open-mouth view to infer transverse ligament rupture and instability
Because the canal is wide at this level, neurological injury is frequently absent
Stable fractures are treated with a rigid collar or orthosis, while transverse ligament incompetence may require halo immobilisation or surgical fixation and fusion
The open-mouth (odontoid peg) view and CT are key, alongside assessment of the atlanto-dens interval
reference.pathophysiology: An axial load transmitted through the occipital condyles onto the obliquely oriented lateral masses of the atlas forces them apart, fracturing the ring at its weakest points where the arches join the lateral masses. Lateral displacement of the masses tensions the transverse atlantal ligament, which may rupture or avulse its bony attachment. Because the fracture tends to enlarge rather than narrow the canal, the spinal cord is usually spared, but loss of transverse ligament competence renders the atlantoaxial articulation unstable and threatens later displacement.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated posterior arch fracture of the atlas
additionalInvestigations: CT of the cervical spine to define the ring fracture and lateral mass displacement
Application of the rule of Spence to lateral mass overhang
MRI to assess the integrity of the transverse atlantal ligament
CT or MR angiography for suspected vertebral artery injury
redFlags: Rupture of the transverse atlantal ligament indicating instability
Lateral mass overhang exceeding the rule-of-Spence threshold
reference.prognosis: Isolated stable atlas fractures usually unite with immobilisation and a good outcome; transverse ligament incompetence signifies instability that may require fusion, but neurological injury is uncommon because the canal is capacious.
pitfalls: Failing to assess the competence of the transverse atlantal ligament
Missing the fracture on plain films by not obtaining CT
Misjudging stability and under-treating an unstable injury
references: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
management: Determine stability from the integrity of the transverse atlantal ligament, which governs treatment choice
Rigid cervical collar or orthosis immobilisation for stable fractures with an intact transverse ligament
Halo vest immobilisation or surgical atlantoaxial fixation and fusion when the transverse ligament is incompetent
Assess for and manage associated vertebral artery injury with CT or MR angiography and antithrombotic therapy as indicated
Analgesia and strict spinal precautions during initial stabilisation and imaging
Spinal surgery referral with follow-up imaging to confirm bony union
